teaser: A basin, a pitcher and four hands: Cassatt paints tenderness from above, the way a Japanese print would.
review_notes:
Dimensions 100.3 x 66.1 cm and 1910 purchase by the Art Institute (Robert A. Waller Fund): check.
Cassatt's letter urging Berthe Morisot to see the 1890 Japanese print exhibition at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts: check.
Link between 1880s cholera epidemics and French campaigns for regular bathing (argument used by the Art Institute): check.
Cassatt never married and had no children: generally stated.

lesson.text: This canvas stands about one meter high and 66 centimeters wide (roughly 39 by 26 inches). That is close to the height of the small child it shows. Hung on a wall, the scene meets you at nearly the scale of life, and yet you seem to hover above it, as if you had just stepped into the room and looked down.

Nothing dramatic is happening. A woman holds a little girl on her lap and washes her feet in a basin. Mary Cassatt, an American from Pennsylvania who made her career in Paris, built much of her work on moments like this one. The question she kept asking was how to paint affection without turning it into sugar.
Her answer here is in the hands. There are four of them, and each one does a different job. Follow them one by one, and the whole relationship between these two people appears.

lesson.title: Four hands
lesson.text: No one speaks, no one looks at us. The hands carry the story.

spots.title: The washing hand
spots.text: The woman cups the small right foot in the water. Her fingers wrap it completely. The gesture is firm and practiced, the grip of someone who has done this many times.

spots.title: The holding hand
spots.text: Her other hand spreads wide across the child's waist. It is large against the small body, and it keeps the girl from sliding off her lap.

spots.title: The bracing hand
spots.text: The child pushes down on the woman's knee to steady herself. She is not passive: she takes part in her own balance.

spots.title: The copying hand
spots.text: The girl's other hand presses on her own thigh, close to the towel. Her arm runs parallel to the woman's arm beside it, like a small echo of the adult.

lesson.text: Did you notice where both of them are looking? Down, at the same spot in the water. Because their eyes are lowered, we cannot meet them. We are watching a private moment that would go on exactly the same if we left.

In the spring of 1890, Paris hosted a huge exhibition of Japanese woodblock prints. Cassatt went back again and again, and wrote to her friend the painter Berthe Morisot that she must not miss it. The next year she made ten color prints of her own in that spirit, one of them a mother bathing a child.

Those prints taught her things Western painting rarely did: to look at a scene from high up, to tilt the floor toward the viewer, to let flat patterns sit side by side without deep shadows. Three years later she carried all of this into oil paint. The lines of this picture show how.
Three shapes hold the composition together.

lines.label: The shared gaze
lines.text: The two heads touch at the top, and both gazes drop along the woman's arm to the foot in the basin. Your eye makes the same descent.

lines.label: The basin
lines.text: From above, the basin becomes a wide oval. A viewer standing level with it would see only a thin sliver. This is the high viewpoint borrowed from Japanese prints.

lines.label: The stripes
lines.text: The broad stripes of the dress run in diagonals that change direction with every fold. They describe the body underneath without any heavy shading.

lines.label: The floor line
lines.text: The floor ends very high, about a third of the way down. Everything below is rug, tilted up like a backdrop behind the figures.

lesson.text: Count the patterns now that you have seen the structure: striped dress, flowered wallpaper, a painted chest at the upper right, a geometric rug, a sprig of flowers on the pitcher. Five of them, crowded together. Against all that busyness, the child's bare skin is the one calm, plain area, and so it glows.
Cassatt made intimacy modern by borrowing from Japanese prints: a view from above, a tilted floor and flat patterns, with all the feeling carried by gestures.

The subject was also of its time. France had lived through cholera epidemics in the 1880s, and doctors were urging families to wash children regularly. A scene that reads as timeless today showed, in 1893, an up-to-date idea of good care.

Cassatt painted children for decades, yet she never married and had no children of her own. She often hired models, and the woman in such pictures is not necessarily the child's mother. The title here says only “the child's bath.”
One last detail hides in the liveliest part of the rug. Cassatt had to put her name somewhere, and she chose a place where it almost dissolves into the weave.
Cassatt signed this painting. Can you find her name?

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: “Mary Cassatt,” written in dark strokes across the rug at the lower left. The letters look like part of the carpet pattern, so the eye passes over them.

lesson.text: The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting in 1910, while Cassatt was still alive. It was a homecoming of sorts: she had spent nearly her whole career in France, exhibiting with the Impressionists at the invitation of Edgar Degas, and American museums were only beginning to collect her.
The water itself is barely painted. Inside the basin, a few strokes of pale blue and white over the grey ground are enough. Your mind supplies the rest, helped by the pitcher standing next to it.

quiz.question: From what angle do we see the scene?
options: Exactly at the child's eye level
quiz.explanation: The high viewpoint turns the basin into a wide oval and tilts the floor.

quiz.question: What event in 1890 marked Cassatt's art?
options: A large exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris
quiz.explanation: She visited the Paris exhibition of Japanese woodblock prints many times.

quiz.question: Where are the woman and the child looking?
options: Down at the foot in the basin
quiz.explanation: Both lower their eyes to the same spot in the water.

quiz.question: Where did Cassatt sign the painting?
options: On the rug at the lower left
quiz.explanation: Her name blends into the carpet pattern at the lower left.

quiz.question: Why does the child's skin stand out so strongly?
options: It is the one plain area among many patterns
It is lit by a candle
quiz.explanation: Stripes, flowers and rug surround the only calm surface in the picture.

facts.text: The Child's Bath is about one meter tall.
facts.explanation: It measures roughly 100 by 66 cm, close to the height of a small child.

facts.text: Cassatt used her own daughter as the model.
facts.explanation: She had no children and often hired models.

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting during Cassatt's lifetime.
